# Chagas disease

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Zoonoses and vector-borne diseases > Chagas disease*

[Original Article Link](/library/EL08zg)

---

## Summary

Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis) is an infectious disease caused by the <u>protozoan</u> <u>parasite</u> <u>Trypanosoma cruzi</u> (<u>T. cruzi</u>), which is typically transmitted by <u>triatomine</u> bugs of the <u>Reduviid</u> family. Chagas disease is <u>endemic</u> to Central and South America and most cases that occur in the US are reported in immigrants from <u>endemic</u> regions. Patients present initially with <u>fever</u>, swelling at the site of <u>inoculation</u> of <u>triatomine</u> feces, and <u>generalized lymphadenopathy</u>. These symptoms resolve within a few weeks, and the patient enters an asymptomatic latent phase, which may last for 10–20 years. Eventually, 10–30% of all infected patients enter a chronic phase and develop symptoms of Chagas <u>cardiomyopathy</u> and/or gastrointestinal disease characterized by <u>achalasia</u> and progressive dilation of the <u>colon</u>. The disease is diagnosed by thin and thick <u>peripheral smears</u> in the acute phase and by <u>serological tests</u> in the chronic phase. Chagas disease patients are treated with the antitrypanosomal drugs <u>benznidazole</u> and <u>nifurtimox</u>. Supportive therapy is required for Chagas <u>cardiomyopathy</u> and gastrointestinal disease. <u>Treatment of Chagas disease</u> is most effective when initiated early (in the acute phase).

## Epidemiology

* <u>Global</u> <u>statistics</u>
* <u>Prevalence</u>: 8–10 million infected individuals; <u>endemic</u> in Central and South America

* <u>Prevalence</u> in the US: > 300,000 infected individuals

## Etiology

* <u>Pathogen</u>: : Trypanosoma cruzi

* Route of infections

* <u>Vector</u> transmission

* Numerous triatomine species of the <u>Reduviidae</u> family (also called <u>kissing bug</u> because it typically bites around the mouth)

* <u>T. cruzi</u> is shed in the feces of the <u>reduviid</u> bug; feces is then rubbed into the bite site while scratching.

* Contaminated food and drinks  [[1]](/library/iNbJa8)[[2]](/library/QNbua8)

* Transplacental transmission from the mother to the fetus

* <u>Blood transfusion</u>, <u>solid organ transplantation</u>

## Clinical features

* <u>Incubation period</u>: 1–2 weeks

* Acute phase (acute American trypanosomiasis): lasts ∼ 8–12 weeks 

* <u>Fever</u>, <u>malaise</u>, loss of appetite

* Cutaneous manifestations

* Chagoma: inflammatory <u>edema</u> at the bite site (usually in the face)

* Romana sign: unilateral painless <u>edema</u> of the eyelids and periocular tissue

* <u>Generalized lymphadenopathy</u> and <u>hepatosplenomegaly</u>

* Rarely (∼ 1% of cases): <u>myocarditis</u>, <u>meningoencephalitis</u>

* Indeterminate phase

* Patient enters an asymptomatic latent phase.

* Patients in the indeterminate phase are serologically positive but do not develop signs and symptoms associated with the chronic phase.

* Chronic phase (chronic American trypanosomiasis): develops after ∼ 10–20 years 

* Chagas <u>cardiomyopathy</u> 

* Conduction disorders: <u>right bundle branch block</u> (<u>RBBB</u>)

* Biventricular dilative <u>cardiomyopathy</u> → <u>heart failure</u>

* <u>Atrophy</u> of the apex, which may lead to <u>ventricular aneurysm</u>

* Mural <u>thrombi</u> → <u>stroke</u>

* <u>Gastrointestinal tract</u>
* Damage to the <u>submucosal</u> and myenteric plexus → inability to relax <u>lower esophageal sphincter</u> and impaired gut motility → progressive dilation of the <u>esophagus</u> and <u>colon</u>

* Megaesophagus and <u>achalasia</u>: <u>dysphagia</u>, weight loss, <u>regurgitation</u>

* <u>Megacolon</u>: abdominal <u>pain</u>, chronic <u>constipation</u>

## Diagnosis

* <u>Confirmatory tests</u>

* Acute phase

* Best initial test: direct visualization of <u>T. cruzi</u> <u>trypomastigotes</u> in thin and thick <u>peripheral blood smears</u> using a <u>Giemsa stain</u>

* <u>PCR</u> to detect <u>T. cruzi</u> <u>DNA</u>

* Indeterminate and chronic phase: serological assays to detect <u>IgG antibodies</u> against <u>T. cruzi</u>

* Additional tests

* Regular <u>ECG</u> monitoring  
* Patients with symptoms or <u>ECG</u> signs of Chagas <u>cardiomyopathy</u> → see “<u>Diagnostics of dilated cardiomyopathy</u>”

* Patient with symptoms of GI involvement: barium <u>radiography</u>, endoscopy, and manometry (also see “Diagnostics” in <u>achalasia</u>)





> [!TIP]
> Chagas disease should be suspected in immigrants from <u>endemic</u> regions.




![Trypanosoma cruzi](media/xxi8amk99z3kap5bwtoidu3k.jpg)

Trypanosoma cruzi

## Treatment

### Antitrypanosomal therapy




Treatment against Chagas disease is most effective when initiated early (in the acute phase).




* First-line: benznidazole (generates <u>free radicals</u> that cause <u>DNA damage</u> in the <u>parasite</u>)

* Second-line: <u>nifurtimox</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Chagas disease is caused by the kissing bug and treated with nifurtimox or Benznidazole: “I'm blowing charming kisses from my nifty Benz.”




### Supportive therapy



* Chagas <u>cardiomyopathy</u>

* See “Therapy of <u>dilated cardiomyopathy</u>.”

* Patients with severe <u>cardiomyopathy</u>: <u>heart transplantation</u>



* Gastrointestinal disease 

* Megaesophagus: see “Therapy” in <u>achalasia</u>

* <u>Megacolon</u>

* <u>High fiber diet</u> with adequate fluid intake, <u>laxatives</u>, and/or rectal enemas to treat <u>constipation</u>

* Patients with persistent <u>constipation</u>, <u>fecalomas</u>, <u>sigmoid volvulus</u>: rectosigmoidectomy (with either retrocecal interpositioning or end-to-side low colorectal <u>anastomosis</u>)
